analysis.one_liner: Makes clothing manufacturers legally responsible for wage and child-labor abuses by their contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote: it sat in a subcommittee for the final three months of the 104th Congress and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act so that garment manufacturers are civilly liable—jointly and severally—for wage, hour, and child-labor violations committed by the contractors they hire, and subject to the same penalties. It would also create fines of up to $1,000 per employee for failing to keep payroll records, and $10,000 per act (doubled for repeat offenses) for submitting fraudulent payroll records that hide hours worked or wage violations. The bill cites findings that most sweatshop employers violate recordkeeping rules, which prevents the Labor Department from collecting wages owed to workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Garment workers—disproportionately immigrants, many paid below minimum wage or denied overtime—gain a new path to collect back pay, because the brand-name manufacturer is now on the hook alongside the contractor who underpaid them. Law-abiding apparel employers also gain, since the bill's stated aim is to stop underpaying shops from undercutting them on price.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Garment workers and compliant apparel makers

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers become jointly and severally liable to the same extent as their contractors for violations of minimum wage, overtime, child labor, and industrial homework rules [S3].
Workers can collect unpaid wages from the manufacturer even when the contractor who employed them is insolvent or disappears, a common obstacle in sweatshop enforcement [S3].

New civil penalties of up to $1,000 per employee for recordkeeping failures, and $10,000–$15,000 per act for fraudulent payroll records, target the practice the bill says blocks the Labor Department from recovering wages workers are owed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers and contractors who currently rely on low-wage subcontracting bear the new liability and penalties, and the cost of compliance or higher contractor rates would be passed into apparel prices. Contractors who violate wage laws could lose business as manufacturers police them.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would face liability for workplaces they do not directly control, since contractors can violate wage and hour laws without the brand's knowledge; an honest manufacturer could be sued for a contractor's hidden violations [S3].
Higher compliance and liability costs in the domestic garment industry could raise apparel prices or push production offshore rather than improve conditions at home [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is accountability versus responsibility without control: workers gain a realistic way to recover stolen wages because manufacturers are far more collectable than small contractors, while manufacturers argue they can be penalized for misconduct they did not supervise. The bill's own findings acknowledge the mechanism it targets—fake or missing payroll records that defeat enforcement—so the recordkeeping penalties are aimed at a real, documented enforcement failure [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 25, 1996, referred to the House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee, sent to its Workforce Protections Subcommittee in mid-October, and Congress adjourned in January 1997 without any hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. William (Bill) Clay of Missouri introduced the Stop Sweatshops Act of 1996 with 54 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on the day of introduction [S5].
Three weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it stayed for the remainder of the 104th Congress with no further action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Garment manufacturers and contractors kept the existing structure, under which legal liability for sweatshop conditions rests with small contractors who are often judgment-proof, and brands face no civil exposure for contractor violations. Garment workers whose wages go unpaid got no new remedy.

for.name: Rep. William (Bill) Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 54 original cosponsors from the House Democratic caucus and one independent [S1][S3][S4].

for.name: 54 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members of the Congressional Black and Hispanic caucuses from major garment-producing districts [S3][S4].

against.name: House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. William Goodling (R-PA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill—no hearing, markup, or vote—before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: U.S. garment and apparel manufacturers
against.role: Industry subject to the bill's new liability
against.what_they_did: Opposed extending manufacturer liability for contractor wage violations during the 1990s sweatshop debates; their opposition was outside the congressional record on this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 54 cosponsors were Democrats or an independent, with no Republican support in the record, and the Republican-run committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill makes them jointly and severally liable for their contractors' wage, hour, and child-labor violations, ending the practice of insulating brands behind judgment-proof subcontractors. The public cost of that insulation is unpaid wages to garment workers.

Shops paying below minimum wage or faking payroll records face the same penalties as before, plus manufacturers policing them. Workers in those shops would gain back pay the current system fails to recover.
The bill's stated purpose is to stop violators from undercutting compliant employers with an unfair cost advantage, so honest shops gain competitive ground alongside workers.
